opus-5.5.text:
I think the analogy works if you look at what CUDA actually did for NVIDIA. CUDA wasn't valuable just because it was software. It lowered the barrier for people to use GPUs. Before CUDA, if you wanted to do general-purpose computing on a GPU, you had to pretend your problem was a graphics problem. CUDA opened that up, and then a whole ecosystem grew on top of it: libraries, researchers, startups, and eventually deep learning itself. The platform made the hardware useful to many more people.

I see Nemotron and Cosmos playing a similar role for the next era of AI. Today, if you want to build an AI application, especially in physical AI like robotics or autonomous vehicles, the hardest part often isn't the GPU. It's that you need a strong foundation model to start from. Training one from scratch is enormously expensive. You need huge amounts of curated data, a lot of compute, and a lot of know-how about data pipelines, tokenizers, and training recipes. Most companies, and even most research labs, can't do that.

So with Cosmos, our world foundation models, the idea is that we pre-train on a very large amount of video, learning how the physical world evolves, and then release the models openly, along with the tools: the data curation pipeline, the tokenizers, the post-training recipes. A robotics company doesn't need to start from zero. They take Cosmos and fine-tune it on their own data, their own robot, their own environment. They can use it to generate synthetic data, to evaluate policies, or as a starting point for their own policy model. Nemotron does something similar on the language and reasoning side: open models, open data, open recipes that enterprises can customize and own.

That's where the CUDA analogy comes in. CUDA became foundational because it was a layer everyone built on, and it kept improving, so the ecosystem compounded. If Nemotron and Cosmos become the default starting point, the layer developers reach for when they build agents or physical AI systems, they become infrastructure in the same sense. The value isn't in any single model checkpoint. It's in the ecosystem and the fact that people can build on it with confidence.

Openness matters a lot here too. Physical AI is still very early. Nobody has a ChatGPT moment for robotics yet. In a field this early, I think the fastest way forward is for many people to experiment in parallel. If we keep the foundation closed, only a few groups can push the frontier. If we open it, thousands of teams can try different ideas, and the whole field moves faster. That's good for everyone, and of course it's also good for NVIDIA, because all of this ultimately runs on accelerated computing. Our incentive is to make the pie bigger, not to own every application.

So I wouldn't say they *are* the new CUDA today. CUDA took more than a decade to become what it is. But structurally they play a similar role: lowering the barrier, enabling an ecosystem, and making a new kind of computing accessible to many more people. That's what we're aiming for.

r001.rationale: The response says CUDA lowered barriers to GPU computing and enabled an ecosystem, but does not describe it as translating application logic into GPU computation.

r002.rationale: It presents Nemotron and Cosmos as foundation models developers can customize and build agents or physical AI systems on top of, making them a potential foundation layer for future software.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When I think about CUDA, what made it so powerful was not the GPU itself. It was that CUDA became the layer every developer built on top of. Once researchers wrote their code in CUDA, once every framework and every library depended on it, the ecosystem itself became the moat. The hardware got faster every generation, but the software layer was what kept people coming back.

Now, in the AI era, I believe the equivalent of that layer is the foundation model. Developers no longer start from scratch. They start from a model and build on top of it. So the question for us at NVIDIA was: what are the foundation models that developers will build on for the next decade?

Nemotron is our answer for language and reasoning. It is an open family of models, and the key word is open. Developers can download it, fine-tune it, distill it, and deploy it anywhere. Just like CUDA, we are not trying to own the application. We want to be the platform underneath the application. If a startup or an enterprise wants to build its own agent, it should be able to take Nemotron, adapt it to its data, and ship it, and the whole stack runs best on NVIDIA.

Cosmos is the same idea, but for the physical world. Language models learned from the internet. But robots, autonomous vehicles, and industrial systems need models that understand physics, space, time, and how objects move and interact. That data does not exist on the internet in the same way, so we built world foundation models that can simulate and predict the physical world. A robotics company can use Cosmos to generate training data, to test a policy in simulation, or to serve as the backbone of the robot's own reasoning.

So the parallel to CUDA is really about position in the stack. CUDA sat between the chip and the application. Nemotron and Cosmos sit between the compute and the intelligence. If a developer's workflow begins with our models, the same way it began with CUDA for the last fifteen years, then the ecosystem compounds. Every fine-tune, every tool, every benchmark built around them makes the platform stronger.

The other thing I would say is that this only works if we are genuinely useful and genuinely open. CUDA succeeded because it solved real problems for scientists before it became a business advantage. We have to earn that same trust with Nemotron and Cosmos. We release the weights, we release the training recipes, we publish the data pipelines. If the community adopts them because they are the best tools available, then they become infrastructure. And infrastructure is what CUDA is.

r001.rationale: The response describes CUDA as a software layer between chips and applications, but does not say it translates application logic into GPU computation.

r002.rationale: It says developers now start from a foundation model and build on top of it, presenting that as the basis of future AI software.

astra-6.text:
I think the analogy is about becoming a foundation that other people build on. CUDA gave developers a common platform for accelerated computing. Once people built libraries, applications, and expertise around it, its value went well beyond any individual piece of hardware.

Nemotron and Cosmos could play a similar role in AI. Nemotron can provide a foundation for building intelligent agents—systems that reason, use tools, and carry out tasks. Cosmos addresses the physical world: helping systems understand and predict how the world changes, which is essential for robotics and autonomous machines.

In both cases, the opportunity is to give developers reusable capabilities so they don’t have to build everything from scratch. If people build their workflows, tools, and applications around those foundations, you can get that same ecosystem effect.

But I would emphasize “could.” A strong model alone doesn’t make something the next CUDA. It needs to be useful, accessible, and reliable, and developers need to keep finding reasons to build on it. That adoption is what ultimately makes it a platform.

r001.rationale: The response calls CUDA a common platform for accelerated computing, but does not describe it translating application logic into GPU computation.

r002.rationale: It presents Nemotron and Cosmos as reusable AI foundations that developers can build agents, workflows, tools, and applications on top of, capturing AI-on-AI as a foundation for future software.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy is really about becoming a platform that other people build on. CUDA gave developers a common foundation for accelerated computing. As more people adopted it, the libraries, tools, and expertise around it made that foundation increasingly valuable.

Nemotron and Cosmos could play a similar role in AI. Nemotron could provide a foundation for building intelligent agents—systems that reason, use tools, and carry out tasks. Cosmos could provide a foundation for physical AI, helping developers model the world and generate scenarios for training and evaluating robots or autonomous systems.

In both cases, the opportunity goes beyond the model itself. If developers build their workflows around these models, and NVIDIA provides the tools to customize, evaluate, and deploy them, you can get a reinforcing ecosystem, much like CUDA.

But I would emphasize ‘could.’ Having a strong model is only the beginning. Becoming something like CUDA requires sustained developer adoption and a platform that keeps solving practical problems.
